speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As one of the world's busiest ports, Singapore welcomes some 12,000 seafarers daily to our shores.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also have one of the largest ship registries in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore is committed to enhancing the well-being of seafarers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a state party to the MLC, Singapore is obliged to give effect to the amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The proposed Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour Convention) (Amendment) Bill 2016 seeks to amend the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour Convention) Act 2014 and to make a related amendment to the Work Injury Compensation Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 2 expands the scope of a ship-owner's obligation to repatriate a seafarer to include scenarios of abandonment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 3 requires shipowners to have in force the necessary insurance or financial security from approved providers to cover shipowners' obligations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such obligations include the repatriation of a seafarer and the payment of compensation in the event of a seafarer's death or long-term disability due to occupational injury, illness or hazard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 4 empowers the Maritime and Port Authority (MPA)'s Director of Marine to grant and revoke the approvals of financial security providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 7 makes a related amendment to the Work Injury Compensation Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It removes the requirement for shipowners to procure separate insurance if they have already done so under the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour Convention) Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Once the amendments come into force, Singapore-registered ships will be required to carry on board documentary evidence of the necessary financial security for inspection by foreign port authorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similarly, foreign-registered ships calling at our port will have to produce the necessary documentary evidence for MPA's inspection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The seafarer unions and the industry have been consulted, and they are supportive of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The proposed Bill ensures that we have the domestic legislation in place to give effect to the amendments to the MLC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because of our global position, we must take the lead to ensure that we are a hub which is not just efficient, professional and reliable, but one which is also responsible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I stand in full support of this Bill to codify into law the amendments to the Convention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2015, I was appalled to read about the alleged slavery and trafficking in the Thai fishing industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could not believe the human rights atrocities reported, which I thought was inconceivable in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, reports continued to surface on abuses ranging from inhumane working conditions to the systematic cheating of seafarers' wages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And one case linked the death of a Filipino seafarer to a recruitment agency in Singapore, though MOM later clarified that the illegal activities occurred outside our borders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Seafarers are fully dependent on the ratification of international conventions to protect their fundamental rights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The implementation of these conventions will be difficult, especially after these new amendments broaden the responsibilities of shipowners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Singapore is one of the few developed countries among the port states and we should be a shining example, being one of the first to implement the new rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Compared to other port states, we have adequate resources and a strong governance system to ensure the human rights of seafarers are codified and enforced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the spirit of these commendable amendments, I have the following questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 75 Two, will the Ministry be taking additional steps to ensure enforcement of these additional protections, given that seafarers have few opportunities whilst on land to access NGO and MOM aid channels?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I want to say that I am heartened by Singapore's enthusiasm towards responsible business practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Although in the short term, shipowners will have to absorb higher costs for compliance, in the long term, it will ensure business continuity for Singapore's ports.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we face increased competition from growing ports in China, our strict compliance with international law will stand out as a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In our pursuit of flexible, commercially-focused policies, we must continue to raise the profile of the human element in businesses – particularly for industries with a global nature, such as shipping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must continue to recognise that the fundamental protection of a human being cannot be subservient to business objectives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Madam, I stand in strong support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill wishes to introduce the amendments by the ILO to the MLC of 2006.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financial security required will be provided by marine insurance companies like Protection & Indemnity clubs, otherwise known as P&I Clubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall refer to these certificates as MLC certificates for the remaining part of my speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I started work as a lawyer doing crew wage claim work for abandoned crew on board commercial ships in these exact circumstances which have given rise to the amendment to the MLC and, indeed, this enabling Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the second half of the 1990s, many shipping companies from the former Soviet Union countries faced bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the end of the Cold War and the break-up of the USSR, many of these shipping companies had struggled to survive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their crew even had to arrest their own ships to sue for their own unpaid wages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the crew were even emotionally reluctant to sue their companies as they had been sailing with their former state enterprises since the period of communist rule.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, these unpaid wages ran into months and even longer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 76 These days, we still see owners failing to pay crew wages when they run into financial problems, especially with the shipping industry being in the doldrums in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When companies collapse, they can leave crew stranded onboard with wages unpaid and, sometimes, even without funding for repatriation and, in some situations, even without provisions, as fleet management take time to work out solutions for the crew as well as with creditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of us here may have read news of crew stranded onboard many ships all over the world which are owned by the Korean conglomerate, Hanjin.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may take quite a few months to settle these problems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that a local company had a similar experience recently, albeit on a much smaller scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Typically, when a shipowner starts to owe its crew their wages, the crew may still continue to work on the vessel for a little while.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crew will often be alerted to take action when they know that the shipowner has other creditors, as, for example, when the ship receives a claim from trade creditors, or when their family is in hardship after not receiving their wages for some months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are practical reasons why crew may not take action for some time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may not be convenient for the crew, given the way ship operations are run.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vessels have tight turn-around time and may not have much time in port.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Crew may need to man the vessel even when the ship is in port.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In some situations, the master may not grant permission for crew to go ashore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, the owners or their agents may not allow the crew to go ashore and the agents' co-operation is required as they need to get the paperwork from local port authorities and also arrange for harbour launches to go to the anchorages to pick up the crew which can be costly to the crew.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if the crew manages to find a lawyer to file their crew wage claims, there may be competing claims in the same proceedings where a ship is arrested by creditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Crew wage claims may be only one of the competing claims among different creditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If shipowners give up their ships, refuse to pay crew wages and let the ships be sold via judicial sale, all creditors will compete for a share of the sale proceeds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As crew wage claim takes higher priority than other claims, unpaid wages can often affect the claims of other creditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, that does not mean that crew will have it easy and their wages can always be recovered.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, the crew wage contractual documentation may be far from ideal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, crew may be promised additional wages, overtime payment but, unfortunately, for the crew, the documentation from the shipowners supporting such payment may be less than perfect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not uncommon these days to see competing claimants trying to overcome the higher priority which crew wages enjoyed over other claimants, by challenging such payments, often using intimidating and even lengthy Court applications, which come with the implied threat of legal cost, which may effectively pressure crew to settle for a smaller sum than as claimed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Coincidentally, it may also be welcomed by other trade creditors as the crew wage claims may not eat into the judicial sale Page: 77 proceeds of abandoned ships which are arrested.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems rather convenient but, in practice, this will only work if the owners will allow the crew unrestricted access to the insurers, whether by phone, email or shore visits to the offices of insurers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, the owner did not pay the ship managers or manning agents for the crew's wages and, as a result, the latter may delay or fail to pay the crew.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad that, under this Convention, even if the contract is entered into between the crew and manning agents, and not with the owners, the crew can now look to the financial security under this Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Much as this convention is a good and big step in the right direction and will bring comfort and assurance to many seafarers, I can still see some practical limitations, which I hope this Government and the world maritime community can continue to make efforts towards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are a small number of shipowners whose crew may not be paid wages on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may, for example, be paid their full wages at the end of the contract term, which can be a few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meantime, they may be given, say, a small allowance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may use such an allowance to buy daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Often, when such crew try to stop work and return home, often due to unhappiness with poor working conditions, the owners may threaten not to pay their salaries in full.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crew's only option will be to leave the vessel and instruct lawyers to file a claim in Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the crew may not have the funds to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the crew may even have entered into one-sided contracts with manning agents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Included in this category are some fishing fleets, which I understand come into Singapore port for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the crew on these vessels, sadly, this Convention may be academic to them and will not really improve their lot.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is great news, as it would ensure that the crew of more ships can enjoy the security intended under this Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, with regard to crew who are serving on board ships which are not entered with these P&I clubs or on board many more smaller home-trade vessels which are not as well regulated for various reasons, whether crew can enjoy protection under this Convention will depend on whether their ship has the requisite insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not assume that this is a given in all cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crew can only make any claim on the MLC certificates if they are still serving on board.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It brings the Page: 78 possibility of owners repatriating seafarers by giving false assurances that outstanding wages of claims will be paid after repatriation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But once repatriated, the financial security may no longer assist the seafarers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the seafarers will have to engage lawyers to pursue their claims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also understand that all states which are party to this Convention are also obliged to have effective port state control to ensure ships entering its port meet the requirements of this Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some ships which come into Singapore port may come from flag-states which are not signatories.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To ensure consistent protection of crew under these provisions, port-states like Singapore which are signatories to this Convention must carry out consistent enforcement when vessels enter port.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have one of the world's busiest ports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And we have one of the largest ship registries in the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to do our part, both as a port-state as well as a flag-state, to ensure that shipowners comply with the IMO Conventions or regulations and to make this Convention and this Bill work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I feel that there is still more that we can do to improve on the certainty of seafarers being paid their fair wages and being paid in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst other broad terms and benefits, it is important that conditions of their employment are taken care of.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, they must be sufficiently cared for in the areas of health protection, medical care, welfare, accident prevention and, if injury were to inadvertently happen, there must be sufficient assistance given for workplace injury which includes adequate compensation to ensure their long-term survivability.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure seafarers are able to return home safely at no cost in cases of abandonment or repatriation for reasons such as illness, injury, shipwreck, trading in a war zone or if the shipowner fails to fulfil his or her legal obligations to the seafarers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, apart from getting the shipowner to repatriate the seafarer, what further actions can be taken against shipowners who commit such irresponsible acts?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the seafarers be reassured if the terms of coverage by a contract of insurance or other financial security will include all the liabilities included in the Work Injury Compensation Act?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 79 It is equally imperative that the seafarers know their rights and understand what employers' obligations are.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this aspect, there should be greater transparency of cases of how repatriation have been managed by shipowners, awareness of the legislation to the various stakeholders, especially the seafarers, adequate education and easy access for seafarers to reach out for help, assistance and counselling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this aspect, the maritime unions have been and continue to do a great job in representing the concerns of these seafarers, especially when they are stranded at sea.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The legislation now makes it even more concrete of their obligations in this aspect.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One must value human lives and workers' rights for fundamental protection, prevention of accidents, incidents and, if it happens, provide both psychological and material support through expeditious treatment, smooth repatriation and fair compensation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this, I am in favour of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, on behalf of our unions and workers in this industry, I wish to raise two issues with regard to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, does the financial security system provide abandoned seafarers with direct access, sufficient coverage and expedited financial assistance?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The amendments have treated the abandonment scenarios envisioned in the MLC amendments as scenarios where shipowners are required to repatriate the seafarer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Do the amendments allow the seafarer to tap on the contract of insurance or financial security to "provide direct access, sufficient coverage and expedited financial assistance" in scenarios of abandonment as envisioned by the amendments to MLC?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can the contract of insurance be tapped on to pay for "necessary maintenance and support" of the seafarer, for example, adequate food, accommodation, drinking water supplies, essential fuel for survival on board the ship and necessary medical care when the seafarer has not been provided with such necessary maintenance and support by the shipowner?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And can the contract of insurance be tapped on to pay outstanding wages to the seafarer when the seafarer has not been paid wages for more than two months?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, is it possible for seafarers to tap on the contract of insurance or financial security when the ship has been arrested or when the shipowner is under receivership?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The shipping industry has been squeezed on both the supply and demand sides: too many vessels, not enough scrapped, while global trade has slowed down.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Container lines are now also in particularly bad shape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Sending a container from Shanghai to Europe costs half what it did in 2014, according to figures from the Chinese city's shipping exchange.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More shipowners are Page: 80 expected to run into difficulties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, the stranded crew of Hanjin Rome, owned by the bankrupt Hanjin Shipping Company, had sat off the eastern coast of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Crew members would have to apply for permission from the Supreme Court to be repatriated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In an arrested ship, at least half the number of officers, engineers and crew or watchmen, security guards must be on board at all times to meet the minimum manning requirement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the case where the ship has been arrested and where seafarers on board have not been provided "necessary maintenance and support, including adequate food, accommodation, drinking water supplies, essential fuel for survival on board the ship and necessary medical care", would the seafarers be able to tap on the financial security system to seek financial assistance in this regard?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the case where a shipowner is in receivership and has not paid its seafarers' wages for more than two months, would the seafarers be able to tap on the financial security system to seek financial assistance in this regard?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Thanaletchimi have spoken from the Labour Movement's perspective; Mr Louis Ng from a humanitarian perspective; and I have found particularly useful from Mr Dennis Tan, speaking from his insights as a very experienced shipping lawyer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I shall attempt to address some of the points that were raised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After all, it is a Convention designed specifically to address the needs of seafarers working onboard ships.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Act today already includes a comprehensive range of employment rights and non-workmen injury compensation for seafarers, which makes it unnecessary to also extend coverage of the Employment Act and Employment of Foreign Manpower Act to seafarers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, the Act provides a seafarer with the right to return home when he decides not to renew his employment agreement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: His trip home will be paid for by his employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay will be glad to know that the provisions in the Bill will allow seafarers to tap the insurance or financial security to pay for such items in case shipowners refuse to or are unable to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the added Page: 81 protection that is currently not available.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it depends on what is in the employment agreement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The same arrangement also applies to ships under arrest or shipowners in receivership.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Should a shipowner face difficulties in tending to his seafarers' needs onboard an arrested ship, the local Court sheriff may arrange for a port agent to tend to the maintenance of the seafarers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, seafarers can have better peace of mind that their well-being is not left to the mercy of the shipowners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The local Court Sherriff can appoint a port agent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On a related note, I am glad to inform Mr Patrick Tay and also Mr Dennis Tan that the seafarers onboard Hanjin Rome, which was the vessel that was arrested in Singapore by its creditors, are in good health and their salaries have been paid on time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is adequate food, water and medical supplies onboard the vessel.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know this because the unions, together with the Maritime Port Authority (MPA), made an inspection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And those who have requested for repatriation were repatriated by the shipowner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Should the owner of an arrested ship like Hanjin Rome renege on their repatriation obligations in future, then the provisions in the Bill will kick in to provide relief to the seafarers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In response to the clarification sought by Ms Thanaletchimi, the insurance or financial security required must provide the same extent of coverage of employers' liabilities as under the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, seafarers are no worse off being covered under the MLC Act instead of under WICA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After the Bill comes into force, MPA will require a ship to carry documentary evidence, or MLC certificates, as Mr Dennis Tan refers to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These MLC certificates must be carried in order to show that necessary insurance or the financial security has been procured.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And the shipowners must also let the seafarers have the contact details of the financial security provider ‒ the Member has already mentioned that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the unfortunate event that a shipowner fails to comply with his repatriation obligations, the affected seafarers may contact the provider directly, or through the MPA, to request assistance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Aside from the provisions in the Bill, I would like to assure Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Louis Ng that MPA has measures in place to deal with irresponsible shipowners or employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Seafarers can use the satellite phone or the Internet onboard the ship to get in touch with MPA to raise any matter of concern.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I know that Mr Dennis Tan highlighted that, sometimes, the shipowners or the ship managers may make things very difficult for the seafarers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is a very valid point, which is why I think it is very important to work with our unions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Work with our unions to educate the seafarers and also to provide to them alternative avenues of feedback, alternative avenues where they can raise their grievances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is something that we take very seriously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Work in partnership with the unions to make sure that the seafarers' rights are not only protected on paper, but that they are, in effect, properly protected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Should any owner of a Singapore-registered ship fall short of fulfilling its obligations, MPA can take Court action to impose financial penalties or even de-register the ship from the Singapore Registry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Furthermore, in its capacity as the port state authority, MPA can inspect all ships calling at Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And a ship may be detained when it is found to be non-compliant with international conventions, including the MLC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And to the point that the Member made, consistent enforcement is absolutely right.
